title: Candle Wax
description: Wax cools as it falls — the brief sting of landing gives way to warmth hardening on skin — and the particular ritual of candle, flame, and not-knowing-where-next is most of what the experience actually is.
equipment: A plain white household candle (not scented, not coloured — these burn hotter), lighter, something to protect the floor
safetyNote: Plain white candles have the lowest burn temperature. Hold at least 45cm above skin — wax cools significantly as it falls. Never use near the face. Have cool water nearby. Test on your outer thigh first.

instructions.label: Solo first
instructions.content: Light the candle, let a small pool form, and drip a few drops onto your outer thigh from 45–60cm up. You're checking whether the brief heat followed by cooling wax produces any response worth exploring.

instructions.label: With a partner (the real version)
instructions.content: Receiver lies back, blindfolded. The giver controls the candle — varying the height (higher = cooler on landing), the pace, and the location across the body. The receiver doesn't know where the next drop will fall. That anticipation — the flicker of the flame, the sound of the wax, the not-knowing — is most of the experience. After one round, switch roles. The giver's experience — controlling the height and timing, watching the receiver's response, choosing where to go next — is a genuinely different thing from receiving.

explore: Solo: is the sensation interesting or just uncomfortable?
As receiver: does not knowing where the next drop lands change things significantly?
Is there something about the ritual quality — candle, warmth, wax hardening on skin — that appeals?
As giver: does controlling the pace, height, and location — and watching the effect — produce its own interest?
why: Wax play combines two distinct nerve responses: the brief, sharp sting of impact and the sustained warmth of wax hardening on skin — these activate different pathways in quick succession. The partner version adds spatial unpredictability, which keeps the receiver's attention fully present between drops without overwhelming it. For some people the sustained hardening warmth is the appeal; for others it's primarily the theatre of the ritual — candle, flame, the visible marks — and both are real draws operating through different mechanisms.
